sentence: Suppose we map every neural correlate of pain with perfect precision. We would still face an explanatory residue: why is there something it is like to be in pain at all? The functional story explains discrimination, avoidance, and report, but it leaves the qualitative felt character untouched. This is the gap that no amount of additional structural detail seems to close, and it is not obvious that calling it an illusion dissolves it rather than renaming it.

Imagine a being physically identical to you, molecule for molecule, yet with no inner experience whatsoever. If such a zombie is genuinely conceivable, then phenomenal consciousness is not logically entailed by the physical facts. Critics reply that conceivability is a weak guide to possibility, since we can conceive of things that turn out impossible on closer analysis. The dispute therefore turns on whether our grip on the concept of experience is clear enough to license a modal claim.

A creature could process information, model its environment, and report its states without any of that processing being accompanied by felt quality. So the question is not what consciousness does but why doing it ever feels like anything. To answer that the feeling just is the doing is to assert an identity, and an identity claim across such an explanatory chasm demands a justification we do not yet possess.

The easy problems concern mechanisms: how attention selects, how memory consolidates, how a system reports its own states. These yield to ordinary scientific methods. The hard problem is different in kind, because solving every easy problem would still leave the question of experience open. That asymmetry suggests the hard problem is not merely harder but structurally resistant to the explanatory style that works elsewhere.

One response holds that experience is fundamental, on a par with mass or charge, rather than derived from anything more basic. This dissolves the demand for a reductive explanation by denying that one is owed. But it purchases that relief at a cost: it must then explain how fundamental experiential properties combine into the unified consciousness of a single mind, a difficulty no less severe than the one it was meant to escape.

Consider the inverted spectrum: two people who agree on every color word yet whose inner experiences are systematically swapped. If this is coherent, then phenomenal character is not fixed by functional role. If it is incoherent, the burden falls on the objector to show why, without simply assuming that experience reduces to function. The thought experiment thus probes whether qualia have any content over and above the relations they enter into.

Even granting that physics will one day describe the brain completely, there is a sense in which such a description would be a structural account: it specifies how parts relate and what they do. Experience, by contrast, presents itself not as structure but as intrinsic quality. The hard problem can be framed as the worry that a complete structural account is the only kind physics can give, and intrinsic quality is exactly what it cannot reach.

To deny the hard problem outright is to claim that once the functional and informational facts are settled, there is simply no further fact about experience. This eliminativist move is consistent, but it asks us to treat the most certain thing we know, that we are conscious, as a confusion. The strangeness of that demand is itself evidence that the problem is not so easily waved away.

Mary, raised in a black-and-white room, knows every physical fact about color vision. On her first sight of red, does she learn something new? If she does, then the physical facts were not all the facts, and phenomenal knowledge outruns physical knowledge. The physicalist must say either that she learns nothing, which seems false, or that she gains only a new ability, which relocates rather than removes the puzzle.

The explanatory gap is sometimes blamed on the limits of human cognition rather than on reality itself. Perhaps a mind built differently could see why neural firing must feel like something. On this view the hard problem is real but soluble in principle, just not by us. That is a humbling thought, yet it still concedes that present concepts leave the connection between brain and experience genuinely opaque.

If every cell in your body is gradually replaced and every belief slowly revised, what makes the person reading this the same person who existed twenty years ago? Bodily continuity fails, since the matter is new. Psychological continuity offers chains of overlapping memory and character, but chains can branch, and a criterion that permits branching cannot ground the strict numerical identity that personhood seems to require.

Suppose a teleporter scans and destroys your body, then assembles an exact replica elsewhere. Did you travel, or did you die while a duplicate began a new life? The case is troubling because every fact about the replica is settled, yet the question of whether it is you appears to remain open. That suggests our concept of identity carries an assumption it cannot cash out.

The fission case is decisive against simple psychological criteria. If your brain were divided and each half placed in a new body, both successors would stand in the relation that supposedly constitutes identity. They cannot both be you, since they are not each other. So either identity is not what matters in survival, or the criterion is wrong, and the more honest conclusion may be the former.

One might hold that the self is not an entity at all but a useful fiction, a bundle of perceptions with no underlying owner. On this view the question of what makes you the same over time has no deep answer because there is no thing whose persistence is in question. Identity becomes a matter of how we choose to bind experiences together, not a fact we discover.

Consider gradual replacement of neurons by functionally identical silicon chips. At no point does anything dramatic happen, yet at the end the brain is wholly artificial. If you survive the whole process, identity tolerates total material change. If you do not, there must be some replacement that killed you, and the absence of any salient threshold makes that conclusion hard to accept.

What matters in survival may come in degrees rather than all or nothing. A future person connected to you by rich memory and continuous character has much of what we care about; one connected by a thin thread has less. If this is right, the question is not whether some later person is strictly identical to you but how much of the relation that grounds prudential concern they bear.

The further-fact view insists that beyond all the physical and psychological continuities there is an additional fact about whether a future person is you, a fact not constituted by those continuities. The trouble is that no one can say what such a fact would consist in or how it could make a difference. A fact with no possible evidence and no functional role looks like a fact about nothing.

If personal identity were what fundamentally mattered, then the prospect of a perfect replica continuing your projects after your death should bring no comfort at all. Yet it does bring some, which suggests that what we care about is the continuation of memory, intention, and character, not the bare metaphysical fact of being numerically the same individual.

A reductionist about persons holds that the persistence of a person just consists in the holding of certain more particular facts, describable without presupposing identity. This is liberating, since it removes the demand for a deep further fact, but it is also unsettling, because it implies that the boundary of the self is conventional, and that the unity of a life is something we impose rather than find.

The puzzle sharpens when we ask about responsibility. If the person who committed an act long ago is connected to the present person only by an attenuated psychological chain, in what sense is the present person the same one who acted? Our practices of praise and blame assume an identity robust enough to bear moral weight, yet the metaphysics struggles to supply anything that robust.

If every event, including every decision, follows necessarily from prior causes obeying fixed laws, then no agent could have done otherwise in the precise circumstances that obtained. The incompatibilist concludes that determinism rules out the freedom required for responsibility. The compatibilist replies that the relevant freedom is not the power to violate causation but the power to act on one's own desires unimpeded, and determinism poses no threat to that.

Adding indeterminism does not obviously help. If a decision is the product of a genuinely random swerve, it is not thereby under the agent's control; it is merely chancy. So the libertarian who hopes that quantum noise rescues free will faces a dilemma: either the noise is irrelevant to the decision or it makes the decision arbitrary. Freedom seems to require something that is neither determined nor random, and it is hard to say what that could be.

The consequence argument runs as follows: no one has power over the laws of nature, and no one has power over the distant past; the present is a logical consequence of those two; therefore no one has power over the present. If sound, this shows that determinism eliminates the ability to do otherwise. Compatibilists respond by reinterpreting that ability as a conditional capacity rather than a categorical one.

Suppose a neuroscientist could predict your every choice from a brain scan taken before you deliberated. Would your sense of open deliberation be an illusion? Not necessarily. The deliberation is itself part of the causal process the scan reflects. Prediction does not bypass your reasoning; it tracks it. The threat to freedom, if there is one, comes not from predictability but from whether the process counts as yours.

Frankfurt cases challenge the link between responsibility and the ability to do otherwise. Imagine a device that would intervene to force a choice, but only if the agent showed signs of choosing differently. The agent chooses freely, the device never acts, and yet the agent could not have done otherwise. If we still hold the agent responsible, then alternative possibilities are not what responsibility requires.

The deepest worry is not about doing otherwise but about ultimate origination. To be truly responsible for an action, one would have to be responsible for the desires and character from which it flowed; but those were shaped by earlier factors one did not choose, regressing to factors before one's birth. This regress suggests that ultimate self-creation is impossible, and with it a certain absolute notion of desert.

Compatibilism can seem like a redefinition that changes the subject. The plain person worried about free will wants to know whether the future is genuinely open and whether they are the true author of their acts. Telling them that freedom merely means acting unconstrained by external force may answer a question, but perhaps not the one they were asking.

If free will is an illusion, our reactive attitudes of resentment and gratitude rest on a mistake. Yet a strict eliminativism about these attitudes may be psychologically impossible and socially corrosive. Some argue we should retain the practices while revising their justification, grounding blame in its forward-looking effects rather than in backward-looking desert.

Source incompatibilism locates the problem not in the absence of alternatives but in the agent's not being the ultimate source of the action. Even in a deterministic world where one could not have done otherwise, what matters is whether the action issues from the agent in the right way. The question then becomes what kind of sourcehood is required and whether determinism precludes it.

Perhaps the dispute is partly verbal. Both sides agree on the facts: the world may be deterministic, agents deliberate, deliberation causes action, and some agents are coerced while others are not. They disagree about which package of facts deserves the honorific 'free.' If so, the substantive questions concern responsibility and control, and the word 'free' is a label whose attachment is the last and least important step.

Every inference from observed regularities to unobserved cases assumes that the future will resemble the past. But that assumption cannot be established by experience without circularity, since any such argument would itself rely on induction. Nor can it be a truth of logic, since a chaotic future is not contradictory. So our most basic mode of empirical reasoning rests on a premise we can neither prove nor do without.

The sun has risen every day on record, yet no number of past sunrises logically guarantees the next. The inference feels overwhelmingly compelling, and that is precisely the puzzle: a habit of expectation can be psychologically irresistible while remaining rationally ungrounded. Hume's challenge is not that induction is unreliable but that we cannot say why it is reasonable.

One reply concedes that induction cannot be justified in advance but insists it can be vindicated: if any method will work, induction will, since it is self-correcting in the long run. Yet 'the long run' is itself a future-directed notion, and the claim that induction will work is the very thing in question. The vindication seems to smuggle in what it set out to provide.

Grue dramatizes the trouble. Define grue as observed-before-now-and-green, or not-so-observed-and-blue. Every observed emerald is both green and grue. The two hypotheses agree on the past and diverge for the future. Induction alone cannot tell us to project green rather than grue, so something beyond observed instances must be doing the work of selecting which predicates are projectible.

If induction has no rational foundation, it does not follow that we should abandon it; we plainly cannot. The lesson may instead be about the limits of justification: some practices are so basic that demanding an external warrant for them is itself confused. To ask for a non-circular proof of induction may be like asking for a proof that proof is reliable.

A pragmatist takes the problem to show that the search for an a priori guarantee was misconceived. Induction earns its keep through success, and success is the only kind of credential an empirical method could have. The skeptic's demand for more than success is a demand for a non-empirical foundation for an empirical practice, and there is no reason such a thing should exist.

Notice that the problem generalizes beyond simple enumeration. Inference to the best explanation, statistical reasoning, and the projection of theories all face the same gap between evidence and conclusion. Whatever defuses the problem for one form of ampliative inference must defuse it for the rest, since they all reach beyond what observation strictly delivers.

Some respond that induction is constitutive of rationality itself: to be rational just is, in part, to weigh evidence inductively. On this view asking whether induction is rational is like asking whether the rules of a game are permitted by the game. The move is attractive but risks making 'rational' a label we award to our own habits.

The deductivist hope is to recast science so that it never infers inductively, only conjectures boldly and refutes by deduction. But even severe testing leaves us with a theory not yet refuted, and the decision to rely on such a theory for prediction is itself an inductive leap. Banishing induction from the logic of discovery does not banish it from the logic of action.

The unsettling possibility is that nature could change its habits at any moment, and no evidence gathered before the change could warn us. We trust uniformity not because we have established it but because a mind that did not trust it could form no expectations at all. The problem of induction may reveal less about nature than about the conditions under which thought about nature is possible.

Consider the hypothesis that you are a brain in a vat, fed precisely the experiences you now have. By construction, every sensory datum is consistent with both this scenario and the ordinary one. If your evidence cannot discriminate between them, then it cannot, on the face of it, justify your belief that there is a hand before you. The skeptical argument needs only this: knowledge requires ruling out the relevant alternatives, and you cannot rule this one out.

The dreaming argument observes that no internal mark distinguishes waking experience from a sufficiently vivid dream. Whatever test you propose, you might be dreaming that you applied it and dreaming that it succeeded. The point is not that you are now asleep but that you cannot, from the inside, certify that you are not. And if certainty about that is unavailable, a certain kind of knowledge of the world seems unavailable too.

One response denies that knowledge requires ruling out every conceivable error. To know there is a table, perhaps you need only that your belief be appropriately caused by the table and that no relevant alternative obtain. The vat scenario, being remote and idle, is not relevant. The skeptic objects that calling it irrelevant is question-begging: its very point is to be undetectable, and undetectability does not entail irrelevance.

Moore famously held up a hand and declared it more certain that here is a hand than that any skeptical premise is true. The strategy is to run the argument in reverse: since the conclusion is absurd, one premise must be false. Whether this rebuts the skeptic or merely refuses to engage depends on whether common-sense certainty can outweigh a seemingly valid argument from seemingly true premises.

A semantic reply argues that if you really were a brain in a vat, your word 'vat' would not refer to vats but to features of your simulation, so the sentence 'I am a brain in a vat' would be false in your mouth. If sound, this shows the skeptical hypothesis is in a sense self-undermining. But it leaves untouched a recently envatted brain, and the worry returns in a slightly altered form.

The skeptic need not claim that we are deceived, only that we cannot rule deception out. This is a modest premise with an immodest consequence. It suggests that the gap between experience and world, once opened, cannot be closed by experience, since any further experience falls on the near side of the gap. The structure of the problem, not any particular doubt, does the damage.

Contextualists propose that 'know' shifts its standards with conversational context. In ordinary contexts, 'I know there is a hand' is true; once the vat is mentioned, the standards rise and the same sentence becomes false. Both the skeptic and common sense are then correct, each in their own context. The cost is that knowledge attributions lose a fixed standard, which some find too high a price for peace.

If the external world is a hypothesis inferred from experience, the inference must be ampliative, and so it inherits all the difficulties of ampliative reasoning. The realist replies that the external world is not inferred at all but is the framework within which inference takes place. Whether that reply is a solution or a refusal to play the skeptic's game is itself a hard question.

Notice the self-locating peculiarity of the vat scenario: it is designed so that its truth would leave no trace in your experience. A hypothesis with that feature can never be confirmed or disconfirmed by you. One might conclude it is therefore not a genuine alternative at all, since alternatives must in principle be distinguishable. The skeptic will say genuineness does not require detectability, and the debate descends to that point.

Even if global skepticism cannot be refuted, it may not need to be lived. The skeptical argument can be granted as a demonstration of the limits of justification while one continues to believe and act as before. This divorces theoretical assessment from practical conduct, which is unsatisfying if we wanted our beliefs about the world to be ones we could fully endorse on reflection.

subtopic: the trolley problem and moral intuition
sentence: A runaway trolley will kill five unless you divert it onto a track where it will kill one. Most judge diverting permissible. Change the case: you can stop the trolley only by pushing a large stranger off a footbridge into its path, killing him to save five. Most judge this impermissible. The numbers are identical; the difference must lie in how the harm is brought about, and articulating that difference is the philosophical task.

subtopic: the trolley problem and moral intuition
sentence: The doctrine of double effect distinguishes harm intended as a means from harm merely foreseen as a side effect. Diverting the trolley foresees the one death; pushing the man uses his death as the means of stopping the trolley. If intention bears moral weight, the cases come apart. But it is strange that the same outcome, brought about by the same agent for the same reason, should differ in permissibility merely by how it figures in a plan.

subtopic: the trolley problem and moral intuition
sentence: A consequentialist sees no real difference: five deaths are worse than one, so both diverting and pushing are required. The widespread reluctance to push is then a moral error, perhaps a useful instinct that misfires in artificial cases. The opponent replies that an instinct this stable and this widely shared is data, not noise, and a theory that overrides it owes us an account of why our intuitions are so reliably wrong.

subtopic: the trolley problem and moral intuition
sentence: The loop variant pressures the means-versus-side-effect line. Suppose the diverted track loops back, so the trolley would still hit the five unless the one body on the side track stops it. Now the one death is a means even in the diversion case, yet many still find diversion permissible. If intuition does not track the intended-or-foreseen distinction here, the distinction may not be doing the explanatory work claimed for it.

subtopic: the trolley problem and moral intuition
sentence: Some argue the relevant factor is agency versus patiency: pushing treats the man as a mere object to be deployed, while diverting redirects an existing threat. To use a person is to fail to respect his separateness, regardless of outcomes. This Kantian thought explains the asymmetry without appeal to intention, by appeal instead to the kind of treatment a person is owed.

subtopic: the trolley problem and moral intuition
sentence: One might distrust the whole method. Trolley cases are bizarre, and intuitions tuned by ordinary life may simply not transfer to them. If the cases are too unlike anything we evolved or were trained to handle, our verdicts about them carry little evidential weight, and building moral theory on them is building on sand.

subtopic: the trolley problem and moral intuition
sentence: Yet the cases earn their keep precisely by being controlled experiments. By varying one feature at a time, they isolate which features our moral judgment is sensitive to. The artificiality is the point: it strips away confounds. The question is not whether the scenarios are realistic but whether the factors they isolate are morally relevant, and that is a question intuition cannot settle by itself.

subtopic: the trolley problem and moral intuition
sentence: The puzzle deepens if our verdicts trace to morally irrelevant features. If pushing feels worse merely because it is up close and physical, then the footbridge intuition reflects squeamishness, not insight. Conversely, if it tracks the difference between redirecting a threat and creating a new one, the intuition is reporting something real. Distinguishing these requires more than consulting the intuition again.

subtopic: the trolley problem and moral intuition
sentence: Whatever one concludes, the trolley problem exposes that our moral thought is not a single coherent algorithm. We deploy consequentialist reasoning, constraints against using people, and distinctions of intention, and these can conflict. A complete moral theory must either show one of these to be fundamental and the others derivative, or explain how they coexist without collapsing into incoherence.

subtopic: the trolley problem and moral intuition
sentence: Notice that the bystander's options are themselves a moral artifact: the scenario presents two choices and forbids a third. Real cases rarely come so cleanly framed. Part of moral skill is recognizing that the way a situation is described already encodes assumptions about what is up to the agent, and the trolley problem, by fixing the frame, brackets that skill in order to examine a narrower one.

Utilitarianism holds that the right act is the one that produces the greatest total well-being. Its appeal is its impartiality: each person's good counts once, no more and no less. But this impartiality is also its difficulty, for it permits, and sometimes requires, sacrificing one person's vital interests whenever doing so yields a larger sum elsewhere. The theory treats persons as locations of value rather than as separate sources of claims.

The objection from separateness of persons holds that summing welfare across individuals ignores a morally crucial fact: there is no super-person who enjoys the total. A burden imposed on one is not compensated by a benefit to another, because the one who bears the burden is not the one who reaps the benefit. Aggregation makes sense within a life, where trade-offs have a single subject, but its extension across lives is what the objection challenges.

Consider whether tiny benefits to many can outweigh a great harm to one. If a billion people each gain a trivial pleasure, may we justly impose torture on a single innocent? The utilitarian arithmetic says yes if the sum is large enough. Many find this monstrous, and the example pressures whether welfare is the kind of thing that can be summed without limit across persons at all.

The repugnant conclusion follows from a plausible-seeming principle: a vast population each with lives barely worth living can have a greater total welfare than a small population of flourishing lives. If only the total matters, the enormous mediocre world is better. Avoiding this conclusion has proved remarkably hard, and the difficulty suggests something is amiss in treating value as a simple sum to be maximized.

Defenders reply that the counterintuitive verdicts are the price of taking everyone's welfare seriously, and rival theories pay worse prices elsewhere. A theory that forbids the sacrifice of one to save many must explain why we may let the many die, which can seem its own kind of monstrousness. The dialectic is not utilitarianism versus common sense but a comparison of which deep cost one is willing to bear.

Average utilitarianism, which maximizes welfare per person rather than the total, escapes the repugnant conclusion but generates its own paradoxes. It can imply that adding a happy person is wrong if she is slightly less happy than the existing average, and that a world of one ecstatic individual is better than a world of billions of merely very happy ones. Each fix to the aggregation function seems to relocate the absurdity rather than remove it.

Rule utilitarianism shifts the calculation from acts to rules: choose the set of rules whose general adoption maximizes welfare, then act on them. This blunts the worry that the theory licenses individual atrocities. But critics charge that a rule utilitarian who would not break a welfare-maximizing rule even when breaking it would do more good has stopped maximizing welfare, and a rule utilitarian who would break it has collapsed back into act utilitarianism.

The demandingness objection notes that if I must always maximize total welfare, then every dollar spent on myself beyond bare subsistence is a dollar withheld from those in greater need. The theory leaves no space for personal projects, no moral room of one's own. Either morality really is this demanding, or a credible theory must make room for prerogatives, and utilitarianism in its pure form makes none.

A subtler worry concerns what well-being is. If it is pleasure, the experience machine threatens the theory, since plugging everyone into blissful illusion would maximize pleasure yet seems a failure. If it is preference satisfaction, malformed or malicious preferences count. If it is an objective list, the theory must defend the list. The aggregation problem presupposes a currency, and the choice of currency is itself contested.

Even granting a currency, interpersonal comparison is fraught. To say one person's gain outweighs another's loss, we must measure welfare on a common scale across distinct subjects. There is no thermometer for happiness, and the assumption that such comparisons are determinate may be a convenient idealization. If welfare cannot be precisely compared across persons, the maximizing project loses its sharp edges.

Deontology holds that certain acts are forbidden whatever the consequences: do not kill the innocent, do not lie, do not break faith. The hard case is the threshold: if keeping a constraint will cost a thousand lives, does it still bind? An absolutist says yes, which can seem fanatical; a moderate allows the constraint to be overridden, which can seem to concede that consequences govern after all. The challenge is to occupy a coherent middle.

A constraint against killing creates a puzzle: it forbids you to kill one even to prevent five other killings. But if killing is bad, should you not minimize killings overall? The deontologist answers that the constraint governs your agency, not the world's total. You are not the guardian of an outcome but the author of your acts, and what is forbidden is your killing, not killing as such.

The distinction between doing and allowing carries great weight for deontology. Killing is worse than letting die, even when the death is the same, because in killing you initiate a fatal sequence while in allowing you merely fail to interrupt one. Critics press cases where the distinction seems to vanish, and the deontologist must show that the line marks a genuine moral joint rather than a mere description of physical proximity.

Kant grounds constraints in the categorical imperative: act only on a maxim you could will as universal law. A maxim of lying for advantage cannot be universalized, since universal lying would destroy the trust that lying exploits. The constraint against lying is thus not a brute prohibition but a requirement of consistency in willing, derived from the bare idea of acting on principle.

The formula of humanity tells us to treat persons never merely as means but always also as ends. To deceive or coerce is to enlist another's agency in a project to which they could not consent, using their rational nature against itself. This explains why constraints attach specifically to persons: it is their capacity for self-governing reason that grounds the demand for respect.

Constraints generate the paradox of deontology: if violating a constraint once would prevent five future violations of the same constraint, the deontologist forbids the violation, thereby allowing more constraint-breaking overall. This looks irrational if constraints express the badness of the act-type. The deontologist must hold that constraints are agent-relative directives, not impersonal goals, and defend that conception of moral structure.

The famously hard case is whether one may lie to a murderer asking where his victim hides. Kant's apparent answer, that lying is forbidden even then, strikes most as a reductio. Yet a deontology that permits this lie may be unable to stop, sliding toward a view on which any constraint yields to sufficiently good consequences. Holding the line somewhere principled is the recurring difficulty.

Deontology can accommodate the intuition that some sacrifices are heroic but not required. Constraints forbid; they do not command optimization. Within the space left by constraints, an agent has prerogatives and may pursue her own life. This gives deontology a structural advantage over maximizing theories: it explains why morality is not relentlessly demanding, because its core is a set of limits rather than a single goal.

An objection holds that constraints are a form of self-indulgence: by refusing to break a rule even to prevent disaster, the agent keeps her own hands clean while letting catastrophe unfold. The deontologist replies that there is a difference between not perpetrating a wrong and being responsible for everything one could have prevented, and that collapsing this difference makes each agent answerable for the whole world's evil.

The deepest question for deontology is what unifies the constraints. Are prohibitions on killing, lying, and promise-breaking instances of a single principle, such as respect for rational agency, or an irreducible plurality? A unified ground promises systematicity and a way to settle hard cases; a plurality may be more faithful to moral experience but leaves the theory looking like a list rather than an explanation.

Virtue ethics asks not which acts are right but what kind of person one should be. The right action is what the virtuous person would do, where virtue is a stable disposition to feel, perceive, and act well. This relocates the primary object of moral assessment from discrete choices to enduring character, and it makes moral knowledge a matter of practical wisdom rather than of applying a rule.

A familiar objection charges that virtue ethics gives no action guidance: telling an agent to do what the virtuous person would do is unhelpful if she does not know what that is. The reply is that all theories ultimately rely on judgment, and that the virtuous person's perception of the salient features of a situation is itself a form of guidance, just not an algorithmic one.

Aristotle locates each virtue as a mean between extremes: courage between cowardice and rashness, generosity between stinginess and prodigality. The mean is not a midpoint on a fixed scale but the response that fits the situation, the person, and the time. Hitting the mean is therefore a skill, sensitive to particulars, and not reducible to a formula that could be followed without perception.

The situationist challenge draws on experiments suggesting behavior depends heavily on trivial situational factors rather than on robust traits. If finding a coin makes people markedly more helpful, perhaps there are no cross-situationally stable virtues at all. Virtue ethicists respond that full virtue is rare and demanding precisely because it is robust, and that the experiments measure ordinary unreflective dispositions, not the trained character the theory describes.

Why be virtuous? Aristotle answers that virtue is constitutive of eudaimonia, the flourishing that is the final end of a human life. Virtue is not instrumental to a separate payoff; it is part of what living well consists in. This grounds the demands of ethics in the agent's own good, avoiding the picture of morality as an external imposition on a self that would otherwise prefer otherwise.

A worry about the eudaimonist grounding is that it makes virtue self-regarding: I am honest because honesty completes my flourishing. But the honest person, on the theory's own account, values honesty for its own sake and for the other's sake, not as a means to her flourishing. The flourishing is a by-product of caring about the right things, not the reason for caring about them.

Practical wisdom is the master virtue that coordinates the rest. Courage without wisdom becomes recklessness; generosity without wisdom becomes a soft touch. Wisdom is knowing what matters here and now, how the virtues bear on this case, and how to act when they seem to conflict. It is not a separate department of knowledge but the intelligence internal to virtue itself.

The unity of the virtues thesis holds that one cannot fully possess any virtue without possessing them all, since each requires the practical wisdom that the others also require. This is striking and contested. It implies that the merely courageous person, lacking justice, is not really courageous but only bold, and that genuine virtue is an all-or-nothing achievement of the integrated soul.

Virtue ethics handles the moral significance of emotion better than its rivals. A person who does the right thing while seething with resentment is, for virtue ethics, falling short, because virtue includes feeling rightly, not merely acting rightly. The fully virtuous agent acts from settled inclination, not from a struggle against contrary desire, and this fit between feeling and action is itself a moral achievement.

A standing question is whether virtue ethics needs supplementing by an account of which traits are virtues. To say a virtue is a trait that contributes to flourishing presupposes a conception of flourishing, and that conception is itself ethically loaded. Without an independent grip on the human good, the theory risks circularity: virtues are what the flourishing life contains, and the flourishing life is the one lived virtuously.

Moral realism holds that there are moral facts as objective as facts about chemistry, true independently of what anyone thinks or feels. The realist must then explain what such facts are made of and how we come to know them, since they are not perceived by the senses and do not figure in physical theory. The anti-realist takes this explanatory burden to be unmeetable and concludes that moral talk does something other than describe.

The argument from disagreement notes that moral views vary across cultures and eras far more than scientific views do, and that moral disputes often resist resolution by evidence. The anti-realist takes this as a sign that there is no fact of the matter. The realist replies that disagreement also persists in disputed empirical and philosophical questions without showing those have no answers, and that moral disagreement may stem from non-moral error.

Expressivism holds that moral statements do not describe facts but express attitudes: to say cruelty is wrong is to voice disapproval, not to report a property. This neatly explains the intimate link between moral judgment and motivation, since attitudes move us as beliefs alone may not. But it must then explain how moral sentences embed in conditionals and arguments, where they seem to behave exactly like ordinary truth-apt claims.

The error theory accepts that moral language aims to describe objective facts but holds that there are none, so all positive moral claims are false. This is a bold and unsettling view: it implies that 'torture is wrong' and 'torture is permissible' are both untrue, the way claims about phlogiston are. Its motivation is that objective prescriptivity, a feature built into moral concepts, is too queer to exist.

The argument from queerness presses that objective moral facts would have to be intrinsically motivating and intrinsically authoritative, unlike any natural fact, and that a faculty to detect them would be unlike any other faculty. The realist can answer either by denying that moral facts have these queer features or by arguing that their queerness is no worse than that of mathematical or modal facts we already accept.

Naturalist realism identifies moral facts with natural facts: perhaps rightness is what promotes well-being, and well-being is itself a natural condition. This makes moral knowledge continuous with empirical inquiry. The open-question argument objects that for any natural property proposed, it remains a substantive question whether what has it is good, suggesting goodness is not identical to any natural property after all.

Constructivism offers a middle path: moral truths are not discovered in a mind-independent order, nor are they mere expressions of feeling, but are the outputs of an idealized procedure of practical reasoning. What is right is what agents would agree to under suitably fair conditions. Whether this counts as realism depends on whether the procedure tracks an independent truth or constitutes the truth it yields.

The companions-in-guilt strategy defends moral realism by noting that the arguments against it, if good, would also discredit mathematics, modality, and epistemic norms, since these too involve non-natural, non-perceived facts. If we are unwilling to be anti-realists about whether modus ponens is valid, consistency may push us toward realism, or at least non-error-theory, about ethics.

Evolutionary debunking arguments contend that our moral beliefs were shaped by selection pressures aimed at survival, not at tracking moral truth, so even if such truths exist, our access to them would be a lucky accident. The realist must show that the forces that gave us moral capacities are not wholly off-track, perhaps because tracking certain genuine values was itself adaptive.

Quasi-realism attempts to earn the right to talk like a realist while being, at bottom, an expressivist. It explains how, starting only from attitudes, a community can build practices of asserting, doubting, and reasoning about moral claims that look indistinguishable from realist discourse. If it succeeds completely, the dispute may dissolve, since the difference between earned and given realism would make no practical difference.

The mind seems to have features no physical thing has: thoughts are about things, experiences have a felt quality, and mental states resist location in space. Yet minds clearly depend on brains. Dualism honors the apparent difference at the cost of explaining interaction; physicalism honors the dependence at the cost of explaining the apparent difference. The problem is that each datum, difference and dependence, undermines the natural account of the other.

If mind and body are distinct substances, how does an immaterial decision move a material arm? Causation across the divide seems to require a shared currency the divide rules out. Descartes located the meeting in the pineal gland, but naming a place does not name a mechanism. The interaction problem is not solved by finding where the two substances touch; it is solved only by explaining how they could touch at all.

Property dualism keeps one substance but two kinds of property, the physical and the phenomenal, with the latter dependent on the former yet not reducible to it. This avoids the worst of substance dualism but inherits a softer version of the interaction worry: if phenomenal properties are not physical, either they do causal work the physical does not, threatening physics, or they do none, making consciousness a passenger.

Epiphenomenalism bites the bullet: mental properties are caused by physical ones but cause nothing themselves, like the steam whistle that signals but does not drive the engine. The view is consistent but deeply counterintuitive, since it implies that my feeling of pain plays no role in my crying out, and, more disturbingly, that my belief in epiphenomenalism is not caused by the experiences it is about.

Functionalism proposes that mental states are defined by their causal roles, not by their substrate: pain is whatever is typically caused by injury and typically causes avoidance, whether realized in neurons or silicon. This explains how the same mental state could occur in very different physical systems. Its limit is the felt quality of experience, which seems to outrun any specification of role.

Identity theory says mental states simply are brain states, as lightning is electrical discharge. The identity is contingent and discovered, not analytic. The objection from multiple realizability presses that if pain can be realized in non-neural systems, pain is not identical to any particular brain state, and identity theory must either restrict its claims or retreat to a more abstract level of description.

Idealism turns the problem inside out: rather than fitting mind into a material world, it holds that what we call matter is itself a structure within or of mind. This dissolves the interaction problem, since there is only one kind of thing. But it must then explain the stubborn regularity and shareability of the physical world, the very features that made materialism attractive in the first place.

Neutral monism posits that mind and matter are two aspects of a single underlying stuff that is in itself neither. This promises to honor both the unity and the duality, but the promise is empty unless something can be said about the neutral base. If the base is characterized only as that which appears mentally and physically, the view risks being a label for the problem rather than a solution to it.

The conceivability of disembodied minds and of mindless bodies has long been used to argue for dualism. But conceivability arguments cut both ways and depend on a tight link between what we can imagine and what is possible. The mind-body problem may be less about which arguments win than about why our concepts of the mental and the physical resist being thought together at all.

Perhaps the problem reflects a limitation of human understanding rather than a fact about reality. There may be a real connection between consciousness and the brain that we are cognitively closed to grasp, just as a dog cannot grasp arithmetic. On this mysterian view, the mind-body problem is genuine and has a solution, but the solution is permanently beyond the kind of mind we happen to have.

A thought can be about Paris, a desire can be for water, a fear can be of nothing actual at all. This directedness, the way mental states reach beyond themselves toward objects, is intentionality, and it is hard to see how any merely physical state could have it. A rock is not about anything. The puzzle is how a brain state, which is also just a physical state, manages to be.

Causal theories try to ground content in causal relations: a thought is about cats because cats reliably cause it. But misrepresentation is a problem, since a thought of a cat can be triggered by a small dog in the dark. If content is what causes the state, the state cannot be false; yet thoughts can be false, so content must be more than its actual causes.

Teleological theories add a normative element: a state means cat if its biological function is to be triggered by cats, even if it sometimes misfires. Misrepresentation becomes malfunction. The difficulty is fixing the function determinately. Was the detector selected to indicate cats, or small moving prey, or warm furry objects? Indeterminacy of function threatens to leave content indeterminate.

Some hold that intentionality is the mark of the mental, the feature that all and only mental states share. Others reply that there is non-derived intentionality in the mind and merely derived intentionality in language and pictures, and that explaining the former is the real task. A map is about a city only because minds interpret it; the mind is about things without anyone interpreting it.

Externalism argues that the content of a thought is not fixed by what is inside the head. Two individuals could be molecule-for-molecule alike yet think different thoughts if their environments differ, because what their words and concepts pick out depends on the world they are embedded in. If so, the mind is not contained by the skull, and meaning is partly a relation to one's surroundings.

Consider a thought that has no real object, such as the dread of a danger that does not exist. Intentionality cannot then be a relation to an existing thing, since one of the relata is missing. This pushes some toward holding that intentional objects are intrinsic contents of the act rather than external items, and the act carries its object within itself even when nothing answers to it.

Conceptual role theories locate content in the inferential connections a state bears to other states: a belief means what it does in virtue of what it is inferred from and what is inferred from it. This explains the holism of meaning but threatens to make content depend on the believer's whole web of beliefs, so that no two people, differing somewhere, ever share a thought.

If physical states have content only derivatively, by being assigned an interpretation, then the content of mental states cannot be derivative in the same way, on pain of regress. There must be something whose aboutness is original. But original intentionality is exactly what no causal, functional, or structural story seems able to deliver, which is why intentionality remains a hard case for naturalism.

The disjunction problem haunts every naturalistic theory of content. Whatever you say a state is reliably caused by, there is a disjunctive alternative it is also caused by, and nothing in the causal facts privileges the non-disjunctive reading. Until a principled way is found to break such ties, the determinacy of what we think will lack a naturalistic explanation.

Eliminativists about content suggest that the very idea of states with determinate aboutness belongs to a folk theory that mature science will discard, as it discarded the humors. If there are no contents, the puzzle of how matter could have them dissolves. But the proposal seems self-undermining, since to assert it is to express a contentful claim, and to argue for it is to deploy contents in inference.

The correspondence theory says a belief is true when it matches the facts. The picture is intuitive but the matching relation resists analysis: what is it for a proposition to correspond to a fact, and what are facts other than whatever makes true propositions true? If facts are individuated by the propositions they verify, the theory threatens to say only that a true proposition corresponds to its being true.

The coherence theory holds that truth is membership in a maximally coherent system of beliefs. It answers the question of access, since coherence is something we can assess from within. But it seems to make truth too cheap: a beautifully coherent fiction would count as true, and there is no evident reason why exactly one maximal system should be coherent rather than many incompatible ones.

Deflationism denies that truth is a substantive property at all. To say a proposition is true is just to assert the proposition; the truth predicate is a device of generalization, useful for endorsing claims one cannot list. If this is right, the search for the nature of truth was misconceived, and the philosophically interesting questions lie elsewhere, in meaning, fact, and reference.

Against deflationism, one may argue that truth plays explanatory roles a mere device of generalization could not. We say that a belief succeeds because it is true, that inquiry aims at truth, that valid argument preserves truth. If these explanations are genuine, truth is doing work, and a property that does explanatory work is not nothing.

The pragmatist proposes that the true is what works, what would be agreed upon at the ideal end of inquiry. This ties truth to inquiry and to consequences. The objection is that a belief can be useful while false and useless while true, so utility cannot be what truth consists in, even if it is often a sign of it.

Any theory of truth must reckon with the liar: the sentence that says of itself that it is false. If it is true, then what it says holds, so it is false; if false, then what it says holds, so it is true. The paradox is not a curiosity but a constraint, since a viable theory of truth must either block the reasoning or pay a principled price for not blocking it.

Truth is plausibly bivalent for ordinary claims, yet vague and future-contingent statements strain bivalence. Is it now true that a borderline-bald man is bald, or that there will be a sea battle tomorrow? If every meaningful claim is determinately true or false, vagueness and the open future become deeply puzzling; if not, classical logic must be revised.

Some hold that truth is one thing in mathematics and another in ethics or comedy, so that what makes a moral claim true differs from what makes an arithmetical claim true. This pluralism accommodates the diversity of discourse. Its difficulty is to explain how a single inference can move validly across domains, mixing premises whose truth would, on this view, be different properties.

The minimalist holds that we grasp truth fully through the schema 'the proposition that p is true if and only if p,' and that nothing deeper underlies it. Every instance of the schema is trivial, yet together they fix the concept. Critics doubt that a concept can be exhausted by an open-ended list of trivialities, and suspect that the schema presupposes rather than explains what truth is.

Whatever theory one adopts, truth seems to be the norm of belief: to believe that p is, in part, to take p to be true, and a belief one knows to be false is barely a belief at all. This normative tie suggests that truth is not just a property beliefs sometimes have but the standard against which believing itself is measured.

Knowledge has long been analyzed as justified true belief: you know that p if p is true, you believe it, and your belief is justified. The analysis is attractive because each condition seems necessary. Gettier showed it is not sufficient: one can have a justified true belief that is true by luck, and luck is exactly what knowledge excludes.

Gettier's cases share a structure. A justified belief is inferred from a false premise yet happens to be true, or a belief is justified and true but the justification connects to the truth only by accident. The lesson is that justification can be present while the believer's grip on the truth is fortuitous, and knowledge requires the grip to be non-accidental.

One repair adds a no-false-grounds condition: knowledge is justified true belief not essentially based on any falsehood. This handles inferential Gettier cases but founders on cases where no false premise is involved, where the believer looks at a real barn but is surrounded by fakes. The luck is environmental, not inferential, so the fix is incomplete.

Reliabilism shifts justification from the believer's reasons to the process that produced the belief: a belief is knowledge if formed by a process that reliably yields truths. This naturalizes knowledge and handles many cases. But the fake-barn case shows reliability must be local, and a process reliable in normal settings can fail to yield knowledge in a deceptive one.

Sensitivity analyses say you know that p only if, were p false, you would not believe it. This elegantly explains why you do not know you are not a brain in a vat, since if you were, you would still believe you were not. But it also seems to deny obvious knowledge, and it can fail to be closed under known entailment, which strikes many as a defect.

Safety reverses the modal direction: you know that p only if you could not easily have believed it falsely. In nearby possible worlds where you hold the belief, it is true. Safety handles the lottery, where you cannot know your ticket will lose because you could easily believe it falsely. Whether safety can be specified without circular appeal to knowledge remains contested.

A more radical proposal holds that knowledge is unanalyzable, a basic mental state more fundamental than belief, with belief understood as botched knowledge. The decades of failed analyses become evidence for this knowledge-first view. The cost is forgoing the project of explaining knowledge in simpler terms, which had seemed the natural ambition of epistemology.

The lottery puzzle exposes a tension. You are highly justified in believing your ticket will lose, far more justified than for many things you claim to know, yet you do not know it will lose. So high probability is not sufficient for knowledge. Something about the statistical, chancy basis of the belief blocks knowledge even when confidence is rationally near-total.

Some argue that knowledge varies with practical stakes: you can know where the bank is when little hangs on it but fail to know the very same thing when much hangs on it, your evidence unchanged. If true, this pragmatic encroachment makes knowledge sensitive to interests, which is surprising if knowledge is meant to track only truth and evidence.

Whatever the correct account, the Gettier problem teaches a durable lesson: knowledge requires that the believer's being right be no accident, that there be a robust, non-lucky connection between the belief and the fact. Specifying that connection without circularity has proven extraordinarily hard, and that difficulty may itself reveal something about how deep the notion of knowledge runs.

subtopic: foundationalism and the regress of justification
sentence: Ask why you believe something, and you cite a reason; ask why you believe the reason, and you cite another. This chain cannot go back forever, cannot loop, and cannot simply stop without warrant, or so it seems. The regress argument forces a choice among infinitism, coherentism, and foundationalism, and each option has long been thought to face decisive objections.

subtopic: foundationalism and the regress of justification
sentence: Foundationalism halts the regress with basic beliefs that are justified but not by other beliefs. The classic candidates are beliefs about one's own present experience, supposed to be self-justifying or incorrigible. The difficulty is that a belief justified by nothing further can look arbitrary, and a belief justified by experience seems to need a further belief that the experience is a good guide.

subtopic: foundationalism and the regress of justification
sentence: Coherentism rejects the linear picture of justification and holds that beliefs are justified by their membership in a mutually supporting web. There are no foundations, only the systematic fit of the whole. The standing objection is isolation: a coherent web might float free of the world, and coherence among beliefs cannot by itself ensure contact with reality.

subtopic: foundationalism and the regress of justification
sentence: Infinitism accepts the regress and embraces an actual infinity of reasons, each justified by the next. The view is logically possible but psychologically strained, since finite minds cannot survey infinite chains. Defenders reply that justification can be a matter of reasons being available, not actually entertained, but critics doubt that an availability never cashed out confers genuine warrant.

subtopic: foundationalism and the regress of justification
sentence: Modest foundationalism weakens the classic claim: basic beliefs need not be infallible, only justified to some degree without resting on other beliefs, and that justification can be defeated by further evidence. This is more plausible than the incorrigible-foundations picture, but it must explain how a non-inferential belief gets any positive justification at all if not from another belief.

subtopic: foundationalism and the regress of justification
sentence: The Sellarsian dilemma sharpens the worry about the foundations. The experience that grounds a basic belief either has propositional content or it does not. If it does, it is itself the sort of thing that can be justified or unjustified, and the regress continues. If it does not, it is hard to see how something non-propositional could justify a belief, which is propositional.

subtopic: foundationalism and the regress of justification
sentence: A response distinguishes the having of a reason from the giving of one. Perhaps a belief can be properly basic if it is formed in the right circumstances by the right faculty, without the believer needing a further belief that the circumstances and faculty are reliable. Justification then becomes a feature of belief formation rather than of a chain of arguments the believer can produce.

subtopic: foundationalism and the regress of justification
sentence: Coherentists can answer the isolation objection by building observational constraints into coherence: a maximally coherent system must accommodate the spontaneous beliefs that perception forces on us. The web is then not free-floating but anchored by inputs it cannot simply ignore. Whether this concedes a kind of foundation, in the privileged status of observation, is a question coherentists must face.

subtopic: foundationalism and the regress of justification
sentence: One might reject the regress argument's framing. Perhaps justification is not always a matter of having reasons one can articulate. A belief may be justified because it is the default until challenged, with the burden falling on the doubter rather than the believer. This shifts the regress: not every belief needs a positive credential, only those that have come under specific suspicion.

subtopic: foundationalism and the regress of justification
sentence: The regress problem may be less a problem to be solved than a map of the options for the structure of justification. Each escape route, foundations, webs, infinite chains, or default entitlement, encodes a different picture of what it is for a belief to be in good standing, and choosing among them is choosing a conception of epistemic order itself.

Two apples are both red, two triangles both three-sided. They share something, and the sharing seems real, not invented. The realist concludes there exists a single entity, redness or triangularity, present in each instance. The nominalist resists positing such repeatable entities and tries to account for resemblance using only particular things. The dispute is about what the world must contain to make sameness of type possible.

Platonic realism places universals in a realm of their own, outside space and time, with particulars participating in them. This explains how the same property can be wholly present in many places at once: it is not, strictly, in space at all. The price is a second realm and the obscure relation of participation, plus the question of how spatial minds grasp non-spatial forms.

Aristotelian realism keeps universals but locates them in their instances: redness exists, but only as the redness of red things, never uninstantiated. This avoids a separate realm. It struggles, though, with universals that happen never to be instantiated, and with the claim that one and the same entity is wholly present in each of its many bearers.

Resemblance nominalism dispenses with universals and explains shared character by resemblance among particulars: red things form a class because each resembles the others. The objection is that resemblance is itself a repeatable feature, a universal in disguise, and that the theory cannot, without circularity, say what makes the right resemblances the relevant ones.

Trope theory occupies a middle ground: properties are real but particular, not universal. This redness here and that redness there are two distinct tropes, exactly resembling but numerically different. Sameness of type is then exact resemblance among tropes, and a concrete object is a bundle of tropes. The view trades repeatable universals for a primitive resemblance among particularized qualities.

Class nominalism identifies a property with the class of its instances: to be red is to belong to the class of red things. But classes are extensional, so coextensive properties would be identical, and if every creature with a heart had a kidney, having a heart would be the same property as having a kidney, which is false.

The one over many argument is the realist's central move: when many things are F, there is one thing, F-ness, that they all are. The nominalist denies the inference, holding that 'a and b are both F' need not commit us to an entity F-ness any more than 'a and b both exist' commits us to an entity, existence.

Predicate nominalism says things share a property simply because the same predicate applies to them: red things are alike in that 'red' is true of each. The obvious worry is that this gets the order of explanation backwards. The predicate applies because the things are red; they are not red because the predicate applies.

Universals would explain not only shared character but also the lawlike connections between properties. If laws are relations among universals, then it being a law that all F are G is a fact about F-ness and G-ness themselves. Nominalists owe an account of natural law that does not quantify over such repeatable entities, and giving one has proven hard.

The deepest question is whether the problem of universals is a discovery about the world or a choice about how to describe it. Realists treat the existence of universals as a substantive fact; some deflationists suspect the whole dispute trades on taking the grammar of predication too seriously, mistaking a feature of language for a feature of reality.

We say things could have been otherwise: the coin could have landed heads. To make sense of such claims, philosophers invoke possible worlds, ways the world might have been. A proposition is possible if true at some world, necessary if true at all. The framework is powerful, but it raises the question of what these worlds are and whether countenancing them is a discovery or a useful fiction.

Modal realism takes possible worlds with full seriousness: they are concrete universes, as real as ours, spatiotemporally and causally isolated from each other. This gives a clean reduction of modality, since necessity becomes truth across a domain of existing things. The cost is an extravagant ontology, an infinity of cosmoses, accepted for the sake of theoretical economy in analysis.

Against modal realism stands the incredulous stare: it is hard to believe there really exist talking donkeys and blue swans, just elsewhere. The realist replies that the stare is not an argument and that the benefits in theory outweigh the affront to common sense. The dispute exposes how much weight intuitions about existence should carry against systematic gains.

Ersatzism keeps the framework but deflates the worlds: possible worlds are not concrete universes but abstract representations, maximal consistent sets of propositions or states of affairs. There is only one concrete world, ours, and the others are abstract ways it might have been. The challenge is to specify these abstracta without covertly relying on the very modal notions they were meant to explain.

Trans-world identity asks whether the very same individual exists across worlds. Could Caesar himself have been a baker? If individuals are world-bound, the question is malformed. Counterpart theory answers that what is true of Caesar in another world is true of his counterpart there, a distinct individual who resembles him most. This makes modal claims about individuals oddly comparative.

Some necessities seem to hold not by logic but by the nature of things: water is necessarily H2O, gold necessarily has its atomic number. These metaphysical necessities are discovered empirically yet hold in every possible world. They suggest that the space of possible worlds is shaped by the essences of natural kinds, not merely by what is logically consistent.

The distinction between de dicto and de re modality matters here. To say it is necessary that the number of planets is even differs from saying of the number of planets that it is necessarily even. The first concerns a proposition; the second attributes a modal property to an object. Possible-worlds semantics renders the difference as a difference in the scope of the modal operator.

If possible worlds explain modality, what explains which worlds there are? The space of worlds cannot itself be contingent without inviting a regress, and saying it is necessary uses the very notion under analysis. Modal realists and ersatzers alike must say something about the modal status of the framework, and any answer threatens to make the explanation presuppose its target.

Counterfactuals are naturally analyzed with worlds: 'had the match been struck, it would have lit' is true if, in the closest worlds where it is struck, it lights. This requires a similarity ordering among worlds, and specifying that ordering without circularity is delicate, since which similarities count seems itself to depend on causal and lawlike facts.

Modal skeptics suspect the whole apparatus answers a pseudo-question. They grant that we make modal claims and reason with them but deny that this commits us to an exotic plurality of worlds. On a deflationary view, to say something is possible is to say no more than that it is, in some sense, allowed; positing worlds to back this is to reify a façon de parler.

We say the short circuit caused the fire, but what does causing add to mere succession? Hume found in causation no necessary connection, only constant conjunction and an expectation in the mind. Yet we surely mean more than that fires regularly follow short circuits; we mean the one made the other happen. The puzzle is to say what that making consists in.

The counterfactual analysis proposes that c caused e when, had c not occurred, e would not have occurred. This captures the difference between causes and mere correlates and explains why we cite the spark rather than the oxygen. But it stumbles on cases of redundant causation, where a backup cause would have produced the effect anyway, so the counterfactual fails though the cause is real.

Preemption is the hardest case. Two assassins, one fires first and kills the victim; the second would have killed him had the first not fired. The first shot caused the death, yet had it not occurred, the death would still have happened, courtesy of the backup. The simple counterfactual gives the wrong verdict, and repairing it without ad hoc patching is notoriously difficult.

Regularity theories hold that causation is instantiation of a law-like generalization: c causes e when c and e fall under a regularity. This honors Hume but struggles with the asymmetry of cause and effect, since regularities run both ways, and with distinguishing genuine laws from accidental uniformities that happen to hold without supporting causal claims.

Process theories locate causation in physical processes that transmit something, a conserved quantity, from cause to effect. A genuine causal process can carry a mark; a pseudo-process, like a shadow's motion, cannot. This grounds causation in physics rather than in counterfactuals. Its limit is causation by absence: the gardener's failure to water caused the plant's death, yet no quantity was transmitted by a non-event.

Causes and effects are asymmetric: the cause brings about the effect, not the reverse, and we can influence the future by acting now but not the past. Yet the fundamental laws of physics are largely time-symmetric. Explaining the directionality of causation from temporally symmetric foundations is a deep problem, often referred to the asymmetry of entropy or of open systems.

Causation by omission strains every theory. The lifeguard's failure to act caused the drowning; but failures are not events, and an infinity of others also failed to act without being blamed. Counterfactual dependence holds for all of them. What distinguishes the lifeguard's omission seems to be a normative fact about duty, which suggests our notion of cause is partly shaped by interests and norms.

The interventionist account ties causation to manipulation: c causes e if intervening to change c would change e, where intervention is itself characterized causally. This makes causation continuous with experimental practice and handles many tricky cases. The worry is circularity, since the notion of intervention is causal, though defenders argue the circle is not vicious but illuminating.

Causation comes in degrees and kinds: contributing causes, triggering causes, background conditions, enabling conditions. Ordinary causal talk selects one factor as the cause and demotes the rest to conditions, and the selection tracks our interests, what is abnormal, and what we could have controlled. A theory of causation must decide whether this selectivity is part of causation itself or a pragmatic overlay on a neutral relation.

Some doubt that there is a single relation answering to the word 'cause.' Perhaps causation as conceived in fundamental physics, as understood in the special sciences, and as deployed in everyday explanation are distinct, only loosely related notions. If so, the search for the analysis of causation is misguided, and what is needed is a survey of a family of relations bound by family resemblance.

Does time pass, or is passage an illusion? The A-theory holds that the present is metaphysically privileged and that events genuinely become past. The B-theory holds that all times are equally real and that 'past,' 'present,' and 'future' merely mark relations to the speaker, like 'here' and 'there.' Our experience seems to side with the A-theory, but physics and logic press toward the B-theory.

Presentism says only the present exists; the past has ceased and the future is not yet. This matches the intuitive thought that what is over is gone. But it must explain how claims about the past can be true if there is nothing for them to be true of, and how present things can stand in relations to non-existent past ones.

Eternalism holds that past, present, and future events are all equally real, laid out in a four-dimensional manifold. The present is not a special slab of being but simply where one is, as here is simply where one stands. The objection is that this seems to deny the reality of change and to render the vivid flow of time a mere appearance.

McTaggart argued that time is unreal. Change requires the A-series, the running of events from future through present to past. But every event is past, present, and future, which is contradictory; and saying it is each at different times presupposes the very series under analysis, launching a regress. The argument is widely rejected, yet no rejection commands consensus.

The growing-block view splits the difference: the past and present exist, accumulating, while the future does not yet. This preserves the openness of the future and the fixity of the past. But it generates a strange epistemic problem, for if past moments are equally real, how do I know that I am at the growing edge rather than stranded in some long-elapsed now?

If the B-theory is correct, the felt passage of time demands explanation as a feature of experience rather than of the world. Perhaps the impression of flow arises from the way memory accumulates and consciousness updates. The challenge is to explain the vividness of becoming without granting it any place in the temporal structure of reality itself.

The open future raises the question whether statements about contingent future events are now true. If 'there will be a sea battle tomorrow' is already true, the future seems fixed; if already false, equally so. To preserve openness, one might deny present truth-value to such statements, but that requires departing from classical bivalence.

Persistence through time poses its own puzzle. Endurance holds that an object is wholly present at each moment it exists, the very same thing showing up again and again. Perdurance holds that it is spread out in time, with different temporal parts at different times. The bent and straight poker is one object with incompatible properties only if those properties belong to distinct temporal parts.

Time travel, if possible, generates the grandfather paradox: travel back, prevent your grandfather's marriage, and you are never born to travel. Consistency demands that whatever you do, you fail to prevent it. This does not show time travel is impossible, only that a traveler's past is not changeable, which itself reframes what 'changing the past' could even mean.

Whether time could exist without change is an old question. If nothing whatever altered, would time still elapse? Some hold that empty time is conceivable and so possible; others hold that time is nothing over and above the ordering of changes, so that changeless time is incoherent. The answer bears on whether time is a container or merely an abstraction from events.

What is it to say something exists? On one view, existence is not a property that things have, the way they have color or mass, but rather the bare fact that there is such a thing. To assert that lions exist is not to ascribe a feature to lions but to say the concept lion is instantiated. This makes existence a second-order matter, a feature of concepts rather than of objects.

Quine proposed a criterion of ontological commitment: a theory is committed to whatever its variables must range over for its claims to be true. To be is to be the value of a bound variable. This turns ontology into a question about the regimented logical form of our best theories, and what we must quantify over once they are made precise.

The Quinean criterion reframes ontological dispute. To deny that numbers exist, one must show that mathematical claims, when properly paraphrased, do not require quantification over numbers. If no such paraphrase succeeds and mathematics is indispensable to science, then we are committed to numbers whether or not we find abstract objects congenial.

Meinong notoriously allowed for objects that do not exist, such as the golden mountain and the round square, holding that we can think and speak truly about them. Russell rejected this, arguing that apparent reference to nonexistents dissolves under analysis into quantified claims that carry no such commitment. The dispute set the agenda for how language relates to ontology.

Some hold that existence comes in degrees or kinds: numbers exist in a different way than chairs, fictional characters in yet another. Others insist that existence is univocal, a single thin notion, and that the apparent variety reflects differences among the things, not among modes of being. Whether being is one or many is among the oldest questions in metaphysics.

Ontological deflationists suspect that many existence disputes are merely verbal. When one party affirms and another denies that there is a table where particles are arranged tablewise, perhaps they agree on every fact and differ only in how loosely to use 'there is.' If so, the heat of ontological debate may reflect a quarrel over words dressed as a quarrel over the world.

The realist about ontology resists deflation. There is, the realist holds, a fact about what the world fundamentally contains, and getting it right is a substantive achievement, not a choice of idiom. The dispute about composition, whether arrangements of simples ever compose a further thing, is then a real dispute with a real answer, even if it is hard to discover.

Fictional discourse pressures ontological commitment. We say that Sherlock Holmes is a detective and that he does not exist, apparently both truly. Either there are nonexistent objects to bear such properties, or the truths about fiction must be paraphrased so that no commitment to Holmes survives, perhaps as truths about a story rather than about a man.

The special composition question asks under what conditions some things compose a further thing. Universalism says always, so there is an object composed of your nose and the moon. Nihilism says never, so strictly there are only simples arranged variously. The intuitive moderate answer, sometimes, has proven hard to state in a principled, non-arbitrary way.
